issues.legal_issue: A magistrate must not try only lesser offences within the magistrate’s jurisdiction while ignoring a serious offence disclosed prima facie by the evidence that requires trial by a higher court.
material_facts: The accused were tried on a complaint alleging, among other things, that registration receipts had been withdrawn using forged endorsements.
The evidence prima facie supported forgery and use of forged receipts, which the court considered capable of constituting the principal serious offence; the other offences were subsidiary.
The magistrate declined requests to commit the case for trial by the Court of Session and tried only offences within the magistrate’s jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The magistrate should have considered the evidence, framed a charge for the serious offence prima facie disclosed, and committed the accused for trial by the Court of Session rather than selecting only offences within the magistrate’s jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the principle that a magistrate must apply the correct law to the facts disclosed by the evidence, even if the complaint does not cite the relevant offence. A charge under sections 467 read with 471 of the Indian Penal Code, if prima facie made out, required commitment under Chapter XVIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure because the offence was triable by the Court of Session.

predicates.criminal_complaint_trial: A criminal court conducts a trial arising from a complaint.
predicates.evidence_supports_serious_forgery: The evidence at trial prima facie supports that a serious forgery-related offence occurred.
predicates.serious_offense_requires_higher_court_tr: The serious offence supported by the evidence is one that the trial court cannot try and that requires trial by a higher court.
predicates.magistrate_omits_serious_offense: The magistrate declines to charge the serious offence and proceeds only on offences within the magistrate’s jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a complaint trial presents prima facie evidence of a serious offence requiring a higher court’s trial, and the magistrate omits that offence, the magistrate must frame the serious charge and commit the case.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may set aside an acquittal and order a retrial when the evidence prima facie discloses a serious offence omitted from the charge and the justice of the case requires intervention, even if the trial court had jurisdiction over the offences it did try.
material_facts: The complainant appealed the acquittal under section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The evidence prima facie disclosed a serious forgery-related offence that had not been charged and that, if charged, would have required trial by the Court of Session.
The magistrate had tried the accused on other offences within the magistrate’s jurisdiction, but had declined to commit the case despite requests to do so.
The High Court set aside the acquittal and ordered proceedings aimed at committing the accused for trial by the Court of Session.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had jurisdiction to set aside the acquittal and order a retrial in these circumstances; the appeal was dismissed. The power must be used with great care, sparingly, and when the justice of the case requires it.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 417 and 423 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court has discretion to order a retrial in an appeal against acquittal. The circumstances warranting retrial are not confined to a fixed list: Rajeshwair Prasad Misra v. State of West Bengal explained that the Code leaves the discretion broad; Abinash Chandra Bose v. Bimal Krishna Sen and Ukha Kolhe v. State of Maharashtra did not limit that power. The court approved Dr. Sanmukh Singh Teja Singh Yogi v. Emperor and held that prima facie omission of a serious offence, particularly one that would have displaced the trial court’s jurisdiction, can justify setting aside an acquittal and ordering retrial when justice clearly demands it.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: A complainant brings an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.evidence_supports_serious_offense: The evidence prima facie supports a serious offence.
predicates.serious_offense_omitted_from_charge: The serious offence supported by the evidence was not included in the charge at trial.
predicates.offense_would_exceed_trial_court_jurisdi: Trying the serious offence would have required a court other than the court that conducted the trial.
predicates.justice_requires_intervention: The circumstances make intervention necessary in the interests of justice.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the evidence prima facie supports a serious omitted offence that the trial court could not try, and justice requires intervention, the High Court may set aside the acquittal and order a retrial.
